fable-5.1.text:
So, self-play is interesting for a reason that is maybe obvious but worth stating clearly. The appeal of self-play is that it gives you a way to turn compute into data. You don't need the data to already exist somewhere in the world. The agent plays against itself, or against copies of itself, and the opponent is always exactly as strong as you are. So you get an automatic curriculum. You're never in a situation where the task is trivially easy or hopelessly hard. That's why AlphaGo worked. That's why Dota worked. You can just keep going, and keep going, and the thing keeps getting better.

But I think there's a more important question, which is: what does self-play actually teach you? And the honest answer is that it teaches you whatever the game is about. If the game is Go, you become extremely good at Go, and not very good at much else. The incentive is very narrow. Now, people had a hope, and I had this hope too at some point, that if you did self-play in a sufficiently rich environment, with many agents, you would get something that looks like general intelligence coming out of it. Because the agents would need to develop all sorts of skills to deal with each other. Negotiation, cooperation, some kind of theory of mind. I think there is something to that. But the environment has to be extremely rich, and it turns out the richest environment we have is the actual world, which is hard to simulate.

The other thing I would say is that self-play is really a special case of a more general question, which is: how do you produce a learning signal once you've used up the signal that nature gave you? Self-play is one answer. It's a very elegant answer for competitive games with a clear winner. I'm less sure it's the answer for what we actually care about, which is models that generalize the way people generalize. A person doesn't need to play a million games against themselves to become competent at something. So there's something about how people learn that self-play, at least in the form we know it, doesn't capture. And I think that gap is where the interesting problems are right now.

r001.rationale: It says self-play turns compute into data and that the data need not already exist in the world.

r002.rationale: It says self-play teaches whatever the game is about, giving Go as an example of becoming good at Go but not much else, and describes the incentive as narrow.

r003.rationale: It does not mention adversarial LLM evaluation or evaluators incentivized to find mistakes.

opus-5.5.text:
Self-play is interesting because it offered a way to create models using compute only, without data. If you believe data is the ultimate bottleneck, then anything that turns compute into capability without new data is very attractive. That's what made it so exciting.

The thing is, self-play as it was done in the past, where you have agents competing with each other, is only good for developing a certain set of skills. It's too narrow. It's good for negotiation, conflict, certain social skills, strategizing. If you care about those skills, self-play will be useful. But it doesn't obviously give you the broad, general capability we actually want.

I'd say self-play did find a home, just in a different form. Think about debate, or prover–verifier setups, or an LLM-as-a-judge that is incentivized to find mistakes in another model's work. It isn't exactly self-play, but it's a related adversarial setup, and people are doing it. I'd see self-play as a special case of a more general idea, which is competition between agents.

And there's one more thing about competition I find interesting. If you have several agents working on the same problem and they can see what the others are doing, the natural response is to try to be different. If everyone takes the same approach, there's no point. So competition creates pressure toward diversity of approaches, and diversity is something current models lack. They all come out of very similar pre-training and end up thinking in very similar ways. So the adversarial, multi-agent direction is valuable not only for the data it generates but also because it might help you get genuinely different ideas.

r002.rationale: It says competing agents are “only good for developing a certain set of skills” and describes this as “too narrow.”

r003.rationale: It describes an LLM judge incentivized to find mistakes in another model’s work as a related adversarial setup.

fable-5.text:
Self-play is interesting. The reason self-play is interesting is that it offers a way to convert compute into data, and that's a very appealing property. If you look at the big self-play successes — TD-Gammon back in the day, AlphaGo, Dota — in all of these cases, you had agents that generated their own curriculum. The opponent is always exactly at your level, so you always have a gradient to learn from. You're never stuck playing against someone too strong or too weak. That's the magic of it, and it's why self-play systems could reach superhuman performance in their domains with no human data at all.

But I think it's important to see the limitation too. Self-play, at least in its classic form, applies to a particular kind of situation — competitive, symmetric games, where you can play against a copy of yourself and the result is meaningful. That's a narrow slice of all the things we want intelligence to do. If you're trying to learn to prove theorems, or to do a long, complicated engineering project, or just to understand the world, it's not obvious what the self-play setup is. There's no opponent in the same sense.

Now, I'd say there's a broader interpretation where the idea stays relevant. You could argue that evolution itself was a kind of giant multi-agent self-play process — organisms competing with other organisms created the pressure that produced intelligence in the first place. And you can imagine that something analogous happens with AI: agents negotiating, collaborating, competing with other agents, and that interaction producing certain skills — social skills, strategic skills, maybe a kind of theory of mind — that would be hard to get any other way.

So my assessment would be: as a complete recipe for intelligence, self-play is not it. But as one component — as a way of generating challenge and curriculum without a human in the loop, for the particular skills where competition is the right framing — I think it's genuinely valuable, and probably underexplored relative to how much attention pre-training has gotten.

r002.rationale: It characterizes classic self-play as suited to a narrow set of competitive, symmetric games and says competition applies only to particular skills.

opus-5.text:
Self-play is interesting for one specific reason, and it's worth being precise about what that reason is. It gives you a way to create a limitless supply of problems that are exactly at the edge of your current ability. Your opponent is as strong as you are, by construction, so the difficulty tracks your competence automatically. That's a very desirable property, because the hard part of any curriculum is that if the task is too easy you learn nothing, and if it's too hard you learn nothing. Self-play solves that for free.

The limitation is that the skills you get are the skills the game rewards. In a competitive game between two copies of the same agent, the pressure is to out-negotiate, out-maneuver, out-deceive the other copy. We saw this in Dota, and in the simpler environments—the sumo wrestlers, hide-and-seek—where you get these quite impressive emergent strategies. But the strategies are about the other agent. You don't get a lot of pressure toward understanding the world, because the world in those settings is extremely thin. The agent becomes socially sophisticated in a narrow way and knows nothing else.

So the question becomes whether you can keep the curriculum property while making the environment rich enough that the skills you acquire are the skills you actually want. I think that's the real research question, and it's unsolved. Debate-style setups, or anything where one copy proposes and another copy verifies, are appealing because verification is often easier than generation, and that asymmetry is a kind of free energy you can extract. But it only works where verification is actually reliable. Where you can't check the answer, self-play tends to find agreement rather than truth—the two copies share all the same blind spots, so they'll happily converge on something wrong and reinforce it.

I'd say self-play was a genuine idea, it was not the central one, and the part of it that matters—automatic difficulty matching—we still want and still don't have a good general version of.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Self-play is interesting because it's a way to turn compute into data. Normally you're limited by the data you can collect, and with self-play you can generate as much experience as you can afford to compute. That was the appeal of the early work, like the Dota 1v1 bot at OpenAI and then AlphaZero, where the agent starts from nothing and gets very strong just by playing against itself.

It's also worth asking what self-play is good for. You put agents in an environment where the opponent is always about as capable as they are. The task is then always at the right difficulty. It never gets too easy or too hard, and as the agent improves, the challenge improves with it. In principle that gives you an open-ended process, because the thing you're competing against keeps getting more sophisticated.

In its pure form, though, it mostly teaches you the skills that competition rewards: strategy, negotiation, deception, social reasoning, and how to model another agent who is also modeling you. Those matter, but they aren't everything. If you want a model that knows facts about the world or can do a particular kind of reasoning, self-play alone won't give you that. It's better understood as one ingredient than as a complete recipe.

I think the more general idea behind self-play is going to matter more than the specific game-playing form of it. That idea is that you have models interacting with each other in an adversarial or cooperative setup, where one generates something and another checks or challenges it. Debate-style setups, or a prover and a verifier, are variations on that theme. It's the same principle: you create the pressure by having the system compete against a version of itself, instead of relying on a fixed dataset.

There's also an evolutionary angle I find suggestive. There's some evidence that social competition was a major driver of brain size and intelligence in primates and early humans. If so, it makes sense that competition among similar agents would produce a kind of intelligence that's hard to get any other way. So I'm optimistic about it, but I'd want to be careful about where it applies.

r002.rationale: It says pure competitive self-play mostly teaches skills competition rewards and that these skills are not everything; self-play alone will not provide world facts or particular reasoning abilities.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think self-play is one of the most important ideas we have, and one of the most misunderstood. Its appeal is that the system generates its own training signal, so you aren't limited by a fixed dataset of human examples. If the environment lets you tell good outcomes from bad ones, and the agent can play against copies of itself, the difficulty rises on its own. AlphaZero is the clearest example. It wasn't taught Go strategy directly. It got there by playing itself.

The catch is that self-play works beautifully when winning is crisp. Games have unambiguous rewards. The real world is messier. For language models, it's not obvious what the opponent is or what counts as a win. If a model just argues with itself about open-ended tasks, it can drift toward strategies that score well on its own judge and nothing else. So the hard part isn't the loop itself. It's building a reward signal that stays honest as the policy gets stronger.

I also don't see self-play replacing pretraining. It complements it. Pretraining gives you a broad prior about the world, and self-play is a way to get past the ceiling of pure imitation. The open question I find most interesting is diversity. Self-play is powerful when the population keeps producing new challenges. If it collapses into one style, it stops teaching you anything.

So my overall view is that it's promising and still underexplored relative to its potential. The bottleneck is reward design and evaluation more than the mechanics of the loop.

astra-6.text:
I think self-play is a very powerful idea. The thing that makes it attractive is that, as you become better, your opponent becomes better, so you keep getting a harder problem. You have this automatic curriculum. And potentially you can turn more computation into more training experience without needing a person to produce that experience for you.

But the big question is: self-play at what? If you have a game with a clear outcome, it’s very natural. You know who won. You can improve. But suppose what you want is a system that can do research. What is the game? How do you make sure that getting better at the game corresponds to getting better at research?

You could imagine one system proposing problems and another system solving them, or one system making an argument and another finding flaws. Those seem like useful possibilities. But you need some way of checking that the problems are meaningful and the flaws are real. Otherwise, the systems might become very good at something that doesn’t matter.

So I’m optimistic about the idea. But I think a lot of the difficulty is in designing the activity in which the self-play takes place.

sol-6.1.text:
I think self-play is very interesting because it gives you a mechanism for generating increasingly difficult problems. As you get better, your opponent gets better, so there is always something more to learn.

But the big question is: where does it apply? In a game, it’s clear what you’re trying to achieve. You win or you lose. And getting better at defeating your opponent is precisely what you want. For a more general task, it’s less clear how to set that up. What does it mean to do self-play for scientific discovery? You can propose an answer and have another model criticize it, but then you need some way to tell whether the criticism is correct. Otherwise, the two models might agree on something that has no connection to reality.

So I would distinguish between having models interact, which could be useful in many settings, and having a self-play process that reliably produces progress. The second requires a good objective and a way to judge success. If you can find those, then I think it could be very powerful.

sol-6.text:
I think self-play is a very powerful idea. If an AI can generate challenges for itself, attempt them, and get reliable feedback, then the difficulty can rise with its capabilities. That gives you a way to keep learning without depending entirely on human examples.

The hard part is the feedback. In a game, you know who won. For many real-world tasks, it’s much less clear whether the model has actually improved or has simply learned to satisfy its own evaluator. So I would expect self-play to be an important ingredient, especially where outcomes can be checked, but its usefulness in more open-ended settings depends on finding ways to keep that learning grounded.

The challenge for language models and real-world tasks is defining what it means to win—having a reliable signal for truth, usefulness, or safety is much harder than scoring a game. But wherever you can build that feedback loop, I think self-play is likely to be very important.

luna-5.6.text: I think self-play is an extremely powerful idea, but it works best when there is a clear environment and an objective that can be reliably evaluated. In games, for example, the model can generate its own curriculum and discover strategies that humans would never provide in a dataset. The difficulty is that, for general intelligence, we don’t yet have a sufficiently rich environment or a reliable signal for what counts as progress. If the model is only playing against itself in an imperfect world model, it can reinforce its own mistakes. So I expect self-play to be an important component, but probably combined with interaction with the real world, external feedback, and methods that keep the training signal grounded.
